name: Mog battle

lead: In looksmaxxing slang, to 'mog' someone is to outclass them in appearance. A mog battle is a thread that puts two photos side by side, from friends, rivals or the poster himself, and asks the community who wins.
Threads on looksmax.org carry titles like 'mog battle between my friends' or 'mog battle who mogs', and replies are short verdicts, sometimes with feature-level commentary.

paras: A poster uploads two photos and asks 'who mogs'. Respondents answer with a pick and often cite features such as facial structure.
The format invites blunt, sometimes insulting responses. Opinions vary between voters and depend on photo quality and angle.

chain: Community votes and names standout features
Poster learns what reads strongly and what to work on
angle.text: Mog battles give users comparative feedback on faces and features. They do not change appearance themselves, but participants can use the comments to decide what to work on, and the format gives a benchmark against which changes in photos can be compared over time.

lead: A mog battle is a comparison thread on looksmax.org in which a poster shows two people's photos, or two items, and the community votes on which one 'mogs' (outclasses) the other [1][2][3]. The word 'mog' is core looksmaxxing vocabulary: it describes one person visibly surpassing another in looks, physique or height, and the verb has spread well beyond forums through TikTok and mainstream media [4][5][6].

For users, the thread format is a quick way to see how a face compares side by side and which features voters say stand out. Replies usually name a winner and sometimes comment on specific features, for example a poster pointing to the sphenoid area as the reason one face looked a certain way [3]. Participants who want to improve their appearance can treat the comments as a list of features that other members notice first, then decide what to work on, such as skincare, body fat, grooming, hair or posture.

Threads range from friends and forum members to matchups between well-known users, and the format is also used for jokes, with titles pitting streaming services against each other [7][8][9]. No published research has examined mog battles themselves.

paras: The format asks voters to pick the better-looking of two people. A typical thread has an opening post with two photos and a title such as 'mog battle' or 'who mogs', followed by replies that are brief and informal, for example a one-line choice of 'the second one' [2]. Some replies focus on bone structure features such as the sphenoid region, and posters sometimes ask respondents to explain how they reached a verdict [3].

Variations include battles between friends [3], between named forum members [8][10], between 'pre-ascension' and later photos of the same user, and between very specific feature types such as eye colour [11]. Some titles pair two people with descriptive nicknames or national stereotypes for comic effect [12]. Others, such as a thread comparing two streaming subscriptions, borrow the format as a joke [9].

Wikipedia's entry on looksmaxxing defines mogging as asserting dominance over someone based on appearance, and lists it among the terms used by communities that grew out of the PSL forums [4]. Mental Floss reports that Merriam-Webster describes it as a humorous internet slang term meaning to outclass, and says the word comes from the acronym AMOG, short for 'alpha male of the group', appearing in forums in the mid-2000s to describe one man visually surpassing another, often in height or bone structure [5]. The Daily Dot also traces it to AMOG and says the first documented use was in 2016, with TikTok popularising it from 2021 [6]. The two outlets differ on the date of first use.

Mental Floss also states that the term is rooted in misogyny and grew within the 'manosphere', and describes its wider use on TikTok, in school classrooms and by an Olympic figure skater as evidence of mainstream reach [5]. Related coinages include 'frame mogging' (outclassing someone through skeletal frame or build).

Voters on the forum usually justify a pick with feature-level language drawn from looksmaxxing discussion: bone structure, eye area, jaw, symmetry, skin and hair [3]. Opinions differ between voters, and several threads show disagreement or one-line jokes rather than a clear verdict [2][3]. Photo angle, lens distance, lighting and expression all affect how a face reads, a point regularly raised in the wider rating-thread culture.

Wikipedia notes that the PSL scale used on looksmaxxing forums to rank faces is considered pseudoscientific by critics [4]. Mog battle threads do not use a formal scale; the outcome is a head-to-head vote.

Mog battles are one of several comparison and rating formats on the forum, alongside appearance-rating threads. Many thread titles, for example those pairing a user with another member or a named rival, show the format used for social competition as well as feedback [8][10][13]. Content creators have also staged 'mog wars' on streaming and social platforms, according to Mental Floss [5].

Participants describe benefits such as a second opinion on which features other people notice and a way to compare progress photos, and describe costs such as blunt or insulting replies [2][3]. Because the audience is anonymous and self-selected, votes reflect the preferences of that community.

lore.intro: Members describe mog battles as a quick way to settle who looks better and to get feature-level opinions, and use the format for banter between friends and rivals [2][3][8].

claims.claim: Votes in a mog battle show whose face is objectively better
A particular bone feature, such as the sphenoid, explains why one face outclasses another
Posting in a mog battle helps you learn what to improve
'Mog' comes from AMOG, 'alpha male of the group'

timeline.event: Mental Floss reports the acronym AMOG, the root of 'mog', appearing in online forums [5].
The Daily Dot gives 2016 as the first documented use of AMOG [6].
Looksmaxxing emerges on incel and manosphere forums including PUAHate, Sluthate and Lookism.net, which developed the PSL scale [4].
The Daily Dot reports mogging spreading on TikTok [6].
Business Insider and The New York Times publish looksmaxxing coverage, according to Wikipedia [4].
Many 'mog battle' threads active on looksmax.org [1][2][3][7][8][10].
Mental Floss describes 'mog wars' between content creators and the term reaching school classrooms [5].
